content:
Even as Apple tries to keep its distance from former design chief Jony Ive in its lawsuit against OpenAI, the company may not be able to stop him from getting pulled into the dispute. Here's why.

OpenAI has a chance to make Apple very uncomfortable

Apple has conspicuously avoided mentioning Jony Ive in its lawsuit accusing OpenAI of stealing trade secrets — even though Ive's company, io Products, developed the hardware at the center of Apple's claims through its partnership with OpenAI.

Apple accuses "OpenAI and its co-conspirators of organized, institutional wrongdoing," a description that covers io, which Apple only refers to as "a company co-founded by Mr. Tang and other former Apple executives." Beyond that, the complaint doesn't name Ive, Evans Hankey, or any other former Apple executive — except for Tang Tan and Chang Liu, who are directly accused of wrongdoing.

While it's still too early to say whether Ive will be called to testify, it's a possibility — especially if OpenAI decides to use him to embarrass or discomfort Apple.

This would put Apple in a uniquely delicate position. Since leaving the company in 2019, Ive has been publicly respectful of Apple, with appearances and visits usually carefully orchestrated.

Those occasions have included attending events with Laurene Powell Jobs and ongoing involvement with the Steve Jobs Archive. Earlier this year, Ive wrote a handwritten letter for the archive's "Letters to a Young Creator" series, recalling his time working with Steve Jobs.

Apple has reciprocated, actively revisiting several controversial late-Ive-era decisions, including the MacBook's butterfly keyboard. The attempt to keep some distance from him in the lawsuit fits with that approach.

But once the case enters the discovery phase, Apple won't have full control over who gets pulled in. Given Ive's role in founding io Products and overseeing the hardware project at the center of the case, OpenAI could argue he has relevant knowledge about the product's development process, what information the team had access to, and whether Apple's trade secrets were involved.

Apple would then face the awkward prospect of cross-examining Ive in court, challenging his testimony, or trying to undermine the credibility of the executive who shaped many of Apple's most iconic products.

This isn't the first time Ive has testified in a lawsuit involving Apple. Back in 2012, he gave a deposition in an Apple patent case, answering questions about the company's design processes and early iPhone and iPad prototypes.

Still, testifying for the opposing side could strain the relationship Ive has carefully maintained with Apple — and could also create friction with OpenAI if Ive feels it's unnecessarily dragged him into the dispute to pressure his former employer.

Do you think Jony Ive will get pulled into this lawsuit? Tell us in the comments.
